name: Gluten-free, casein-free diet
short: Autism, restrictive diets (not shown to be this diet): rickets in 11, low-calcium seizures, fractures. Milk-free (allergy): fractures in girls. Casein-free: thinner hand bone. This diet: less calcium.
text: Children with autism: in 75 boys with autism aged 4 to 8, the thickness of a hand bone on X-ray fell increasingly short of reference values with age, and the shortfall was nearly twice as large in the 12% of boys on casein-free diets as in boys on minimally restricted or unrestricted diets (p < .04); the authors advise that bone development be monitored, especially on casein-free diets. In a Spanish comparison of 20 children with autism on the diet and 85 on a regular diet, using 3-day food diaries, those on the diet had lower weight, body mass index and intake of energy, pantothenic acid, calcium, phosphorus and sodium, and needed vitamin D supplementation, though they ate more fibre, legumes and vegetables. A 2021 meta-analysis of six randomised trials (143 children aged 3 to 17) found that the diet might trigger gut adverse effects (relative risk 2.33, 95% CI 0.69 to 7.90, a range that includes no difference). In a study of 75 children with autism and 28 controls, children on elimination diets (the abstract does not say which) had a lower body mass index score than children without dietary restrictions, and only 11.1% had a medical reason for the diet. On the other side, a study of boys aged 4 to 8 found lower spine bone density in boys with autism than in boys without autism, unrelated to elimination diet status or calcium and vitamin D intake; a study of blood vitamin D found no significant difference between 9 boys with autism on a casein-free diet, 40 with autism on an unrestricted diet and 40 controls, although 61% of all the children had low levels; and in a 14-child challenge study, with nutritional counselling, the authors describe the diet as safe and well tolerated. Fractures (a different population): in a case-control study in Poland of children and young people aged 2.5 to 20, a milk-free diet for cow's milk allergy was linked with fractures in girls (29.4% of girls with fractures against 11.8% of controls had followed one; odds ratio 4.6) but not significantly in boys (odds ratio 1.3); the authors say it is uncertain whether this is due to the allergy, the calcium deficit or other milk nutrients, and that the contribution of a milk-free diet to fractures in children and adolescents is modest. Other restrictive diets (not shown to be this diet): two US children with severe food restriction developed iodine deficiency with an underactive thyroid (hypothyroidism), one with a goitre, and both could stop thyroid hormone once iodine levels were normal, in a report that introduces the trend to casein-free and gluten-free diets without saying these children followed one; in a retrospective chart review at one urban children's hospital, 11 children and adolescents aged 4 to 16 with autism and restrictive diets, all from the lowest-opportunity neighbourhoods, had severe nutritional rickets, 8 with very low blood calcium and 3 with seizures from low calcium, and complications included fractures of both thigh-bone necks needing surgery (most improved with nutritional supplements alone; the abstract does not say whether any followed this diet); and a 4-year-old with autism developed scurvy (vitamin C deficiency) from long-term selective eating without fruit or vegetables (a case report). No interaction data were found in the cited sources.
